tldr: To handle negation-constrained grasping instructions like 'grasp the mug by the body, but avoid the handle', this paper introduces a framework that steers particles at inference time (via SMC and CFG) away from forbidden regions without any negative training data.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed approach. (a) A Flow-Matching DiT trained purely on standard positive instructions is combined at inference time with (b) LLM instruction decomposition, Find3D forbidden-region localization, perpendicular CFG, and stochastic SMC with churn to steer grasp poses into safe regions in real time.
overview:
In language-driven dexterous grasping, satisfying negative avoidance constraints—such as 'do not touch the blade' or 'avoid the hot body'—is critical for safety. However, existing training corpora like DexGYSNet contain virtually no negation examples. As a result, existing models suffer from a fatal shortcut: when told 'avoid the handle', they actually attempt to grasp the handle instead.

Collecting training data for every conceivable forbidden constraint is impractical. The authors address this by steering sampling at inference time without any negation training data. First, they build a Flow-Matching Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that jointly updates grasp poses and contact points in continuous space. At inference time, an LLM and 3D part grounding identify the forbidden region. Then, perpendicular Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) pushes candidates away from that forbidden region, and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) prunes candidates heading for violations while replicating safe ones. To prevent replicated particles from collapsing onto identical trajectories, they introduce stochastic 'churn' that injects noise without distorting marginal distributions.

Evaluated on the newly introduced 'NegGrasp' benchmark, this approach reduces the forbidden-region violation rate of the strongest baseline (DextER) from 57.9% to 17.2%, while also improving physical grasp success in simulation.
contributions: Identified that existing language-driven dexterous grasping models fail on negation constraints not due to model architecture, but due to an extreme absence of negation expressions in training data (<0.01%) and a learned word-contact shortcut.

Proposed an inference-time steering method that requires zero negation training, combining contact-prediction-based perpendicular CFG, particle filtering (SMC), and marginal-preserving stochastic churn.
Constructed the 'NegGrasp' benchmark comprising paired positive/negative language instructions and grasps, along with rigorous metrics such as the Constraint-Aware Success Rate (CSR).

sections.heading: Why do existing models touch exactly what they are told to avoid?
sections.summary: Telling a robot 'do not touch here' is natural for humans, but existing models fail completely. Because they are trained only on positive instructions, they mistake any mentioned part for a grasp target. The authors solve this at inference time using particle steering (SMC) and CFG.
sections.details:
Natural language serves as an intuitive interface for multi-finger dexterous manipulation. However, when conventional models like DextER are given negative safety constraints—such as 'grasp the knife by the handle without touching the blade'—they almost always end up touching the forbidden part.

Why does this happen? The root cause is not an architectural defect, but the training data. The widely used DexGYSNet dataset contains virtually no avoidance instructions. Consequently, models learn a shortcut: 'if a part name appears in the prompt, it must be a contact target.' As a result, the instruction 'avoid the body' is misinterpreted as 'grasp the body.'

One could collect negation datasets for fine-tuning, but gathering every possible constraint across all users and situations is impractical. This paper instead focuses on steering the generative trajectory during inference without retraining the model. Using a Flow-Matching DiT that can evaluate and refine candidate poses mid-trajectory, the authors combine Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to steer a model that has never seen a single negation during training toward successful avoidance.

sections.heading: Bringing negative prompting and particle steering from image generation to robotic grasping
sections.summary: The paper connects three research threads: language-driven dexterous grasping, negative prompting in image diffusion, and SMC guidance for diffusion models. Leveraging a generative model that tracks continuous contact points, it adapts perpendicular CFG and stochastic flow sampling to robotic grasping.
sections.details:
This work bridges insights from three main areas:

- Language-driven dexterous grasp generation: Recent studies like DexGYSNet and DextER predict contact locations and joint angles autoregressively from language. However, these models target only positive instructions ('where to grasp') and cannot handle avoidance directives.
- Negative prompting techniques: In image generation, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) subtracts scores of undesirable concepts. Furthermore, perpendicular guidance subtracts only the component orthogonal to the positive direction so that the target task is not canceled out. This work translates that idea to grasp contact velocity vectors.
- SMC-guided diffusion: Research has shown that weighting and resampling particles during diffusion sampling can steer generation toward higher-reward directions. While prior work has guided autoregressive tokens, grasping relies heavily on final geometric arrangements; continuous refinement via diffusion is far better suited than uncorrectable autoregressive generation.

sections.heading: How inference-time steering works: Perpendicular CFG and stochastic SMC
sections.summary: Building on a Flow-Matching DiT trained solely on positive instructions, the method uses an LLM and 3D part grounding at inference time to locate forbidden regions. Orthogonal CFG steers candidates away during sampling, SMC prunes violating candidates while replicating safe ones, and churn maintains particle diversity.
sections.details:
The overall architecture consists of two main stages:

3.1 Grasp Generation Model (Flow-Matching DiT)
Input text is encoded with a frozen Qwen, and point clouds are encoded with a frozen PartField. Fine-tuning these text and geometry backbones causes general visual priors to collapse (Fig. F3), so both are kept strictly frozen. The generated state consists of a 28-dimensional grasp pose (wrist pose + 22 joint angles) and 8 contact slots (3D coordinates + occupancy flags), totaling 9 tokens. These are jointly denoised using a 12-block DiT and Flow Matching (Rectified Flow).

3.2 Instruction Decomposition and Region Grounding
At inference time, an LLM (Gemma 4) first breaks down the raw prompt into a positive instruction A and a forbidden part, constructing positive template B (e.g., 'grasp the mug by the handle'). Next, an open-vocabulary 3D grounding model (Find3D) identifies the point cloud of the forbidden region $\mathcal{F}$ within the object point cloud.

3.3 Gated Perpendicular CFG Steering
At each sampling step, the model predicts the contact coordinates one step ahead (look-ahead) from the current velocity field. If a predicted contact point falls within a threshold distance of the forbidden region (gating), the model computes the difference between prompt A velocity $v_c^A$ and prompt B velocity $v_c^B$. It projects out the component parallel to $v_c^A$ to yield an orthogonal update $g_\perp$, which is added to the contact velocity. Using only the orthogonal component allows sideways avoidance without degrading the primary grasping target.

3.4 SMC, Churn, and Final Selection
Across $N$ parallel particles, look-ahead contact coordinates are scored with a potential $\Phi$ based on distances to the forbidden region and the object surface, followed by resampling. However, running deterministic ODEs causes 'particle collapse', where replicated particles never diverge. The authors introduce a 'churn' step that injects small diffusion noise and drift correction while preserving marginal distributions, preserving diversity across particles. Finally, forward kinematics (FK) reconstructs the hand mesh to select the single best grasp that strictly satisfies all constraints.

sections.heading: NegGrasp benchmark results: Slashing violation rates from 57.9% to 17.2%
sections.summary: Tested against baselines like DextER on the new NegGrasp benchmark, the proposed method dramatically reduced violation rates from 57.9% to 17.2% and boosted Constraint-Aware Success Rate (CSR). Ablations show that CFG, SMC, and Churn act synergistically.
sections.details:
4.1 NegGrasp Benchmark and Evaluation Metrics
By mining DexGYSNet scenes for competing parts where one grasp touches a part but another grasp avoids it, the authors created 6,928 valid negation instances (2,793 test instances across 15 categories). Metrics include Violation Rate (Viol., percentage of grasps contacting forbidden parts), Contact Ratio (Cont.), Clearance margin (Clear.), Constraint-Aware Success Rate (CSR, whether grasps safely touch targets without violations), and Task Success Rate (TSR, measuring physical stability in Isaac Gym).

4.3 Main Results
When presented with raw negation prompts, existing baselines like DexGYS and DextER showed violation rates of 55.3% to 57.9%, essentially ignoring negative constraints. Adding LLM decomposition with Best-of-N (BoN) selection still left a 29.9% violation rate. In contrast, the proposed steering framework slashed violations to 17.2%, achieved a CSR of 61.5% (+5.5 points over baseline), and reached the highest physical Task Success Rate (TSR) at 38.7%.

4.4 Ablation Study
Ablation experiments revealed clear trade-offs and complementary strengths:
- CFG alone: Improves avoidance, but velocity fields deviate from the training distribution, lowering TSR from 38.3% to 31.0%.
- Deterministic SMC added: Restores physical quality (TSR 40.5%), but causes particle collapse (degenerating to 2–5 unique particles out of 16), which pushes violations back up to 28.3%.
- Churn added: Stochastic noise preserves full diversity across all 16 particles, balancing CFG avoidance and SMC physical fidelity (17.2% violation, 38.7% TSR).

sections.heading: Conclusion and takeaways
sections.summary: This work identifies why language-driven dexterous grasping fails on negative constraints and provides an inference-time steering framework that requires no extra negation data. This enables safety-constrained grasp generation without expensive data collection.
sections.details:
This study uncovered the root cause behind why existing language-driven grasp models systematically break under negative constraints, and solved it using inference-time perpendicular CFG, SMC, and stochastic sampling with churn.

Despite using zero negative training examples, the proposed method reduces forbidden-region violations to less than one-third of the strongest baseline while improving grasp stability. This inference-time steering paradigm represents a promising path for seamlessly integrating safety rules and user-specific constraints into future robot foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix: Qualitative comparisons, hyperparameter sensitivity, and implementation details
sections.summary: Qualitative comparisons (Fig. F4) show the method avoiding forbidden parts while generating diverse poses. Sensitivity analysis confirms the choice of churn strength $\eta$ and evaluates computational cost.
sections.details:
The appendix provides thorough supplementary validations:

- Qualitative Evaluation (Fig. F4): For red-highlighted forbidden parts (e.g., knife blades, spray pump heads, camera grips), baselines grasp over the forbidden regions, whereas the proposed method maintains clean clearance. The model also discovers grasp configurations distinct from ground truth, showing it is not merely memorizing patterns.
- Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Performance saturates at $N=16$ particles, offering the best balance with computational cost. Churn strength $\eta$ is the most sensitive parameter; $\eta=0$ suffers deterministic collapse with a 28.3% violation rate, whereas $\eta=0.1$ reduces it to 17.2% (excessive churn distorts trajectories and degrades TSR).
- Runtime and Reproducibility: On four NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPUs, generation and simulation evaluation across all 2,843 test cases took approximately 1.6 hours, scaling linearly with particle count. Statistical bootstrap tests (B=10,000) confirmed significant gains over baselines.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparisons of grasp poses on the NegGrasp test set. For forbidden parts highlighted in red, DexGYS and DextER make contact or attempt grasps, whereas Ours successfully avoids the forbidden parts while grasping the designated regions.

takeaways: Negation expressions ('do not touch X') risk being misinterpreted by positive-only foundation models as an inverse shortcut ('touch X').
Without retraining the model, combining LLMs, 3D open-vocabulary grounding, perpendicular CFG, and SMC can strictly enforce geometric safety constraints purely at inference time.
When applying SMC resampling in diffusion or flow matching, deterministic ODEs cause particle collapse; adding stochastic churn without disturbing marginal distributions is critical.
limitations: Forbidden region identification relies on frozen external tools (an LLM parser and Find3D); if part grounding fails, steering cannot function (occurs in ~1.8% of test cases).
The current parser implementation only targets the first detected forbidden part, lacking support for composite constraints with multiple forbidden regions.
Evaluations are limited to single-object simulation environments (Isaac Gym with ShadowHand); testing in cluttered scenes and on physical robot hands remains future work.
